name: Jamal Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a jumbo underground at Northgate, a nickel mine. A jumbo's a drilling rig with two long arms, booms, that drill the holes in the rock face for the charge-up crew to fill with explosives. You line up the booms, drill your pattern, sixty-odd holes, and get out before they fire. I like it when the face comes down clean. What wears me out is the travel, forty minutes down the ramp in the truck and forty minutes back.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Lisa works part-time in the school canteen, and we've got Adam, who's twelve, and Hana, who's nine. I coach Adam's under-thirteens football on Saturdays. And I've got a shed out the back, paid off, where I fix up old motorbikes and sell them. Made enough last year to pay for the family holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, back to work. I'd tell the lads at crib we can stop worrying about robots. I'm not big online, I'd maybe share something in the football club group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think it's sensible. Things change slowly in mining, they always have. Every new gadget takes years to work properly underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep working, keep saving, keep the motorbikes going in the shed. I'd keep using the AI thing on my phone to look up old parts numbers, because it's quicker than the forums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI to look up motorbike parts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. My mate Gus showed me. I ask it what fits a 1982 trail bike and it saves me an hour of digging. It gets things wrong sometimes, so I check, but it's handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The managers would still chase every cent, AI or not. They'd squeeze us in other ways, more metres per shift, fewer people on the crew. That's the bit that never changes.

S0.say: I'd say that's that, back to work, and tell the lads at crib to stop worrying about robots. I might share something in the football club group.
S0.think: I think it's sensible, because things have always changed slowly in mining. Every new gadget takes years to work properly underground.
S0.do: Keeps working, saving and fixing up motorbikes in his shed. Keeps using an AI app now and then to look up old parts numbers.
S0.quote: Every new gadget takes years to work properly underground.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal sees slow change as normal in mining and is relaxed about the plateau. His motorbike business is a real side income and a source of pride. His grievance is with managers squeezing crews, which he sees as constant regardless of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life, and the ones who work hard and learn will be all right. I'd tell the young lads to get a trade ticket, not just a machine ticket. That's what I'd say at football too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the jumbo's on the list. Northgate's already got one jumbo that can drill a pattern on its own overnight, and the boss loves it. So I'd be watching very carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save more, put off the new ute, and watch to see how the self-drilling jumbo works out. If the first few operators who take the remote course end up all right, I'd take it too. I'd also ask the boss if there's a way to get more hours in maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I wouldn't be losing sleep yet, but I'd be keeping score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if jobs at Northgate went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Management chasing quarterly numbers. Not the robots, they're just tools. And not the government, I don't want them in it. I just want bosses who look further than three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the motorbike shed become more important?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. It's not a living, not yet. But if I had to, I could do two or three more bikes a year. People like old bikes, and they like knowing a real person fixed them.

S1.say: I'd say change is part of life and those who work hard and learn will be all right. I'd tell young lads at work and at football to get a trade ticket, not just a machine ticket.
S1.think: I think the jumbo is on the list, because Northgate already has one that drills a pattern on its own overnight. I'd be watching very carefully.
S1.do: Saves more and puts off buying a new ute while he watches how the self-drilling jumbo works out. Plans to take the remote course once others have done well from it and asks about more hours in maintenance.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not losing sleep yet but keeping score.
S1.quote: I just want bosses who look further than three months.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal waits for proof before acting, which fits his steady nature. He blames short-term managers, not robots or government, and wants government kept out. His motorbike shed starts to look like more than a hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a mess, and those big companies ran ahead of everyone. At work I'd tell people to keep calm and look after their families. I'd not go online, I'd talk to people face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think the jumbos go first and everything else follows. My savings would last a while, and the bikes would give us a bit. But Lisa's canteen job alone won't cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut out everything we don't need straight away. I'd do more bikes in the shed, five or six a year, maybe more. We'd hold off on the kitchen reno and sell my old ute. And I'd sit down with Lisa about whether she could take more hours, though even that might go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach would be in knots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, I'd take it, but I'd not like it. I'd rather earn it. I'd ask my brother first, he's got a farm and might need hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your football team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to keep training and keep showing up, same as always. Kids need something steady. I'd not tell them the world's ending, because I don't know that.

S2.say: I'd say it's a mess and the big companies ran ahead of everyone. I'd tell people at work face to face to keep calm and look after their families.
S2.think: The jumbos go first and everything else follows. Savings would last a while and the bikes would help, but Lisa's canteen job alone won't cover the mortgage.
S2.do: Cuts everything not needed, delays the kitchen renovation and sells his old ute. Ramps up motorbike restoration to five or six a year and talks with his wife about more hours.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with his stomach in knots.
S2.quote: I'd not tell them the world's ending, because I don't know that.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI turns Jamal's side business into a key part of his plan. He'd take government help reluctantly but would turn to family first. His instinct is to stay steady for the kids he coaches, even while alarmed himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair bit of time, if people use it. I'd tell the lads to get a second skill. I'd say it at work and at the football club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd be forty-eight. The house would be nearly paid off. I think I'd get three or four more years at Northgate if I'm lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a heavy diesel mechanic course at the technical college part-time, because someone still has to fix things for a while. I'd keep the bikes going, maybe turn the shed into a proper little business. And we'd pay the house off as quick as we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be busy, and busy's better than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the mechanic course rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm good with my hands and I know engines. It's a trade, a real one, not an app. And it fits with the bikes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years feel different from two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm just holding on. Five years, I can build something. It's like the difference between a quick patch and a proper rebuild.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a fair bit of time if people use it. I'd tell the lads at work and the football club to get a second skill.
S3.think: I'd be 48 with the house nearly paid off. I'd probably get three or four more years at Northgate if I'm lucky.
S3.do: Studies heavy diesel mechanics part-time at the technical college and grows the motorbike shed into a small proper business. Pays off the house as fast as possible.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, which he prefers to worrying.
S3.quote: It's like the difference between a quick patch and a proper rebuild.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Jamal build on what he already knows, engines and bikes, rather than reinvent himself. He picks a hands-on trade that fits his values. His preference for being busy over worrying runs through the interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so no excuses. I'd tell people at work and at the club to learn a trade and work hard. That's how it's always been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three. House paid off, kids nearly grown, the bike business going. I think I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the diesel course over a couple of years, then keep working at Northgate as long as I could. I'd grow the bike shed into a proper business, maybe take on an apprentice. I'd tell Adam to look at a trade, maybe even work with me in the shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It'd be in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprentice? Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how I learned, from an old bloke who knew engines. I'd want to pass that on. It's better than a course on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young blokes who just started at Northgate with big loans on their utes. Ten years of payments and maybe no job at the end. I'd tell them to slow down on the spending.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so there are no excuses. I'd tell people at work and at the club to learn a trade and work hard, as it's always been.
S4.think: At 53 the house would be paid off, the kids nearly grown and the bike business going. I think I'd be all right.
S4.do: Takes the diesel course over a couple of years and stays at Northgate as long as possible. Grows the bike shed into a proper business with an apprentice, and encourages his son towards a trade.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, with the worry in the background.
S4.quote: That's how I learned, from an old bloke who knew engines.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Jamal looks forward to passing on his trade through an apprentice, a very traditional answer to automation. He's confident about his family. His worry for young miners with big loans echoes his own careful approach to money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time to build anything and the bikes alone won't pay the bills. What would help is companies giving real notice and paying people out properly, plus apprenticeships for people my age, not just for kids.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the young ones starting out. They've got the most to lose and nobody's telling them straight. I'd want someone to tell them before they sign up for a big loan.

portrait: Jamal Bauer is 43 and drives a jumbo drill underground at the Northgate nickel mine, coaches his son's football team and restores old motorbikes in a paid-off shed out the back. He uses AI now and then for parts numbers but waits to see changes proven before acting. He blames short-sighted managers rather than robots or government. Calm or uneasy in the milder pictures, he's alarmed by fast AGI and leans on his bike business and family. With more time, he plans a diesel mechanic trade and dreams of taking on an apprentice of his own.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there'd be no time to build anything and the bike business alone wouldn't pay the bills.
whatWouldHelp: Real notice and proper payouts from companies, plus apprenticeships for people his age, not just school leavers.
